dialog.body: Public Works, this is Lorraine. Good evening, how can I help you?

Hi hon, yeah, Declan Hanlon here. I'm calling about the street in front of eighteen Carroll Avenue. Over in the Fifth Ward. Every time we get a real storm it turns into a pond. And I mean a pond, hon. Cars are going through and throwing wakes up onto the sidewalk.
Okay, eighteen Carroll Avenue. And that's the street itself that's holding water, not the inside of a building?

The street. Well, it's the low end, right, where the road dips. All the water runs down and just sits there. I manage the house, so I'm there most days and I see it. It was like that after the nor'easter, Saturday into Sunday, and it's Wednesday now and there's still a puddle you could lose a Corolla in.
Still standing three days later. Okay. Is it blocking the road, or are cars able to get through?

They get through, that's the problem. They go slow at first and then some guy in a pickup comes barreling in and, whoosh, wave over the curb. Nobody's stopping. I'm worried somebody's gonna stall out.

And I called before about this, I want to say last year. Somebody told me it was a state road, so it's not the city's problem. I mean, I'm looking at it, hon. It's got city houses on it, city mailboxes, the whole thing. Who's it belong to?
I hear you. I don't have the earlier call in front of me, so let me make sure I have this right. You were told before that Carroll Avenue is a state road?
That's what I was told. And nothing happened. Again. Same thing every winter, somebody passes the buck and the water sits.
Let me check the road listing while you're on. Can you give me the closest cross street to where it pools?

It's the bottom of Carroll, where it dips down toward the water side. Right in front of eighteen, a little past it. Can't miss it, there's a drain in the gutter that I swear is packed with leaves and muck.

Okay, a drain at the low end that may be clogged, in front of eighteen. [pause] All right, I'm entering it as a storm drain and standing water complaint, and I'll note that it's the low point of Carroll Avenue and that you were previously told it was a state road. I'll have the supervisor look at who maintains that stretch.
Good. Because if it's the state, fine, then you tell me and I'll call them. But somebody's gotta tell me for real this time.
Understood. Whoever owns it, we'll get you a straight answer. Is the best number for you the one you're calling from?
Yeah, four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-six-nine.
Four-oh-one, five-five-five, oh-one-six-nine. And Declan Hanlon, H-A-N-L-O-N?
That's it. Hey, do the crews go out on weekends? Because if it rains again Saturday I don't want to be calling Monday saying the same thing.
They do get called out on weekends when there's flooding on the roads. If it's a real hazard, call the main number and it gets routed to whoever's on.

Okay. Good. Because honestly, it's been like this too long. I got enough going on. The one thing I'm looking forward to is the school holiday program next week, the kids' day thing at the rec center. That's the one thing on my calendar I'm actually excited about.
That sounds like something to look forward to. Okay, so I've got the report in, and someone from the department will call you back about the drain and who's responsible for the road.
Alright, hon. Thanks. I'll be watching the puddle in the meantime.
You have a good night, Mr. Hanlon.
You too. Bye.
